after.authors: Coca-Pulido, A.; Solis-Urra, P.; Martin-Fuentes, I.; Contreras-Rodriguez, O.; Ruiz-Malagon, E. J.; de la Calle, E.; Voss, M. W.; Mora-Gonzalez, J.; Esteban-Cornejo, I.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Physical Education and Sports, Faculty of Sport Sciences, Sport and Health University Research Institute (iMUDS), University of Granada, Granada,
after.abstract: Gait variability and physical fitness may provide accessible indicators of brain health in aging, yet their associations with resting-state dynamic functional connectivity remain unclear. We examined associations of gait variability and physical fitness with local and distant temporal consistency of resting-state dynamic functional connectivity in 86 cognitively normal older adults from the AGUEDA trial. Gait variability was assessed using coefficients of variation for stride length, gait velocity, step time, and step length, while physical fitness included muscular strength and cardiorespiratory fitness. Dynamic functional connectivity was estimated using voxel-wise stepwise connectivity analyses. Analyses targeting regions related to Alzheimers disease risk and exploratory whole-brain analyses were adjusted for age, sex, and education. Greater gait variability was associated with local, but not distant, temporal consistency of dynamic functional connectivity. Greater stride length, gait velocity, and step length variability were associated with higher local temporal consistency in the left inferior frontal gyrus ({beta} = 0.28 to 0.33; false discovery rate-corrected P = 0.024 to 0.047) and lower temporal consistency in the right insula ({beta} = -0.47 to -0.31; false discovery rate-corrected P = 0.001 to 0.028). Whole-brain analyses revealed lower local temporal consistency in the left parahippocampal gyrus with greater stride length variability ({beta} = -0.43; family-wise error-corrected P = 0.002) and in the left calcarine cortex with greater gait velocity variability ({beta} = -0.45; family-wise error-corrected P = 0.001). No statistically significant associations were observed for physical fitness. These findings suggest that gait variability may reflect aspects of local dynamic functional brain organization in cognitively normal older adults.

after.title: Preprint: Genetic variants associated with 90-day survival in sepsis patients
after.authors: Zeggane, S.; Mslmane, A.; Fleuriet, J.; Heming, N.; Bacq-Daian, D.; Olaso, R.; Deleuze, J.-F.; Annane, D.; Garchon, H.-J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Paris-Saclay University, UVSQ, INSERM U1173, Infection and Inflammation Laboratory, Montigny-le-Bretonneux, France
after.abstract: Sepsis is a highly prevalent and life-threatening syndrome resulting from an exaggerated inflammatory response to an infection. Its etiology is multifactorial and involves both environmental and genetic factors that are presently poorly understood. We conducted a genome-wide association study (GWAS) on sepsis patients survival at 90-day following admission in the ICU. We extracted genotypes of single-nucleotide variants (SNVs) from whole-genome sequencing data of 1030 patients from three cohorts, including APROCCHSS, RECORDS-Observational and TRIAL. We used a proportional hazard Cox model adjusted for age, the first two genetic principal components and the cohort. We identified 7 significant SNVs that reached genome-wide significance (P<5 x 10-8). One of them, rs1474684, maps to the last intron of the phospholipase C Beta 1 (PLCB1) gene and likely is causative, following fine-mapping. Two other SNVs map to IMPDH1P7 gene for rs146038228 and CALCRL-AS1 for rs4667156. Both genes lie in a 400 kb region showing extended linkage disequilibrium that prevented resolution of the causative variant. The other four variants were low frequency SNVs mapping to non-coding or intergenic regions near ENSG00000288587 (rs11754929), ENSG00000248172 (rs74570843), ISG20 (rs139793868), and RNU6-144P (rs78812419). Gene Set Enrichment Analysis, a sensitive nonparametric method to rank pathways associated with variants and genes, consistently highlighted terms associated with the central nervous system, synapse physiology and cardio-endocrine regulation. Altogether, our findings shed new light on genetic factors and pathways associated with survival in sepsis patients. However, further investigation in an independent cohort will be necessary for validation of the associations.

after.authors: Leistle, H.; Dadar, M.; morrison, C.
after.abstract: BACKGROUND: Estrogen is thought to be neuroprotective; however, estrogen drops during menopause. Hormone-replacement therapy (HRT) could prevent cognitive decline in females by replacing endogenous estrogen. However, research has generated contradictory findings on whether HRT benefits cognition in females. The current study explores the influence of estrogen-only HRT and estrogen-progestin HRT on cognitive performance in females over time. METHODS: Longitudinal data from 22,706 female participants aged 55+ (n = 1336 estrogen-only HRT, n = 144 estrogen-progestin HRT, n = 21,226 no HRT) was included from the National Alzheimer's Coordinating Center. Linear mixed-effect models examined the relationships between HRT conditions and cognitive functioning over time. RESULTS: Both types of HRT were associated with slower decline in cognition, with combination HRT predicting better cognitive outcomes than estrogen-only HRT. DISCUSSION: The findings suggest that HRT may offer protective effects for cognition over time, especially estrogen-progestin HRT, contrary to some previous research; however, more research is needed.

after.authors: Irfan, A.; Jadoon, K. K.; Hanif, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Ghulam Ishaq Khan Institute of Engineering Sciences and Technology, Topi, Pakistan
after.abstract: Automated twelve-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) interpretation has historically relied on discriminative classifiers limited to closed-set diagnostic labels, signal reconstruction, or saliency heatmaps. While categorizing predefined arrhythmias well, these static classifiers cannot generate narrative clinical reports, incorporate patient history, or support interactive clinical question-answering (Q&A). We present LifeLine.ai, an end-toend multimodal Vision-ECG-Language framework for automated cardiac diagnosis and clinical reporting. After early attempts at waveform peak-tracking and coordinate mapping failed against complex morphological variations, we leveraged large-scale PhysioNet repositories (MIMIC-IV and PTB-XL). Because hardware limits precluded training on over 800,000 raw records, we curated a balanced subset to estimate performance, converting one-dimensional signals into 3x4 twelve-lead grids with continuous Lead II rhythm strips at the bottom. Our pipeline integrates YOLOv11s localization, a LoRAadapted Google SigLIP encoder, a trainable Multi-Layer Perceptron projector, and a 4-bit quantized MedGemma-4B model, complemented by a separate Kahneman-Tversky Optimization (KTO) pipeline built on collected user feedback and a multi-LLM consensus engine. On this compact subset, SigLIP outperformed Swin Transformer encodings (~0.21 vs. ~0.25 validation loss), achieving 71.0% open-vocabulary precision and a 75.0% contextual F1 score across a cloud deployment spanning Vercel, mobile apps, Amazon EC2, Firebase, Hugging Face, Modal GPUs, and lifelinecg-sdk. Our code is available at https://github.com/Asad939asad/ LifeLine.ai-.

after.authors: Lopez Pineda, A.; Tripp, J.; Santana-Quinteros, D.; Flores-Garrido, M.; Garcia-Velazquez, L. M.; Figueroa-Mora, K. M.; Gomez-Garcia, A.; Alvarez-Aguilar, C.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Universidad Michoacana de San Nicolas de Hidalgo
after.abstract: Longitudinal electronic health records (EHRs) from primary care are scarce in low- and middle-income countries, and few have been made available to researchers in Latin America. We present DiabetIA, a longitudinal dataset derived from the primary care records of the Mexican Institute of Social Security (IMSS). The first release comprises 136,674 adults followed in six IMSS family medicine units in the state of Michoacan between 2005 and 2020, with more than 3.2 million visits summarized in 414,770 two-year windows with at least one visit. Each window includes demographics, ICD-10 diagnoses, anthropometry, vital signs, laboratory results and prescriptions, and type 2 diabetes diagnoses in the following year as prediction targets. At baseline, 24.4% of the patients had type 2 diabetes, 37.1% hypertension and 32.3% obesity. Technical validation assessed completeness, plausibility, consistency, temporal coverage and agreement with a state health survey. DiabetIA is freely available for download to support research on chronic disease trajectories and prediction in an underrepresented population.

after.title: Preprint: Retention in care and viral suppression among people on HIV treatment receiving 6- versus 12-month prescriptions in South Africa: a cohort study using routinely collected electronic health data
after.authors: Mokgethi, N. O.; Huber, A. N.; Shumba, K.; Munsamy, M.; Ramdas, N.; Jamieson, l.; Rosen, S.; Pillay, M.; Pascoe, S.; Manganye, M.; Malala, L.; Fox, M. P.; Miot, J.; Mokhele, I.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Health Economics and Epidemiology Research Office, School of clinical medicine, University of the Witwatersrand, Johannesburg, South Africa
after.abstract: Introduction During the COVID-19 pandemic, ART prescription lengths in South Africa were temporarily extended from six months to twelve months for stable clients, reducing required clinic visits from two to one per year. We compared retention and viral suppression outcomes between clients receiving 6-month and 12-month prescriptions within South Africa's Centralised Chronic Medicines Dispensing and Distribution (CCMDD) programme, which serves over 3.2 million people living with HIV through medication collection at facility-based or community-based pickup points. Methods: We conducted a retrospective cohort study in seven South African provinces using routinely collected electronic health data. We included adults ([≥]18) with a 6-month or 12-month ART prescription issued between June and November 2020. Participants were followed for 24 months. Retention was defined as [≥]1 medication collection visit during months 13-24 of follow-up and viral suppression as a viral load <50 copies/ml at the first test conducted in that window. We estimated unadjusted retention and suppression rates and then used a modified Poisson regression model with a log link and robust standard errors to compare non-retention and viral non-suppression between groups, accounting for district-level clustering and adjusting for age, sex, time on ART, model of care, and ART regimen. Results: Among 428,926 clients, 196,531 (46%) received 6-month prescriptions and 232,395 (54%) received 12-month prescriptions. During the outcome assessment period (months 13 to 24), clients in the 6-month group attended a median of 2 clinical prescribing visits and clients in the 12-month group attended a median of 1 clinical prescribing visit. Unadjusted retention was 91.4% in the 6-month group and 91.6% in the 12-month group; viral suppression was 79.3% in the 6-month group and 80.9% in the 12-month group. After adjustment, using the 6-month prescription group as the reference, adjusted risk ratios were 0.98 (0.91-1.05) for non-retention and 0.93 (0.82-1.06) for viral non-suppression. Conclusion: Twelve-month prescriptions maintained retention in care and viral suppression rates equal to 6-month prescriptions while halving required annual clinic visits per client. These findings support further evaluation of reduced-frequency prescribing within differentiated HIV service delivery programmes for stable clients and contribute to the evidence base to guide recommendations on reduced clinical prescribing visits.

after.title: Preprint: One-year outcomes after mass transfers during the first COVID-19 epidemic wave in France. A cohort study
after.authors: Grimaud, O.; Martin, S.; Ricard-Hibon, A.; Pottecher, J.; Philippe, J.-M.; Leray, E.; Bayat, S.; Braun, F.; Carli, P.; Tattevin, P.; Noizet, M.; Sanchez, M.-A.; Dolz, M.; Vuagnat, A.; Maury, E.; Chauliac, N.; Coignard, H.; Prieto, N.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Univ Rennes, EHESP, CNRS, ARENES - UMR 6051, Rennes
after.category: intensive care and critical care medicine
after.abstract: Objectives Even taking into account the selection of healthier patients, it has been shown that the mass transfers of patients between intensive care units (ICUs) outside their own region during the first wave of the COVID-19 pandemic in France was associated with lower mortality but a higher rate of psychiatric disorders in the ICU. In other countries, the survival benefit of such transfers had faded after around 60 days. Our aim was to determine the long-term outcomes (up to one year) associated with these mass transfers in France. Design TRANSCOV retrospective cohort study enriched by data linkage with hospital admissions, outpatient consultations, prescriptions and deaths database. Setting Multi-centre study involving 39 origin ICUs from the East and Paris regions (France) and 57 destination ICUs located in regions then unaffected by the pandemic. Participants Patients with severe COVID-19 (n = 1,113) admitted to ICUs in the Eastern and Paris regions between 4 March 2020 and 10 April 2020. Exposure Being transferred from versus remaining in overburdened ICUs. Outcome measures The main outcome was death occurring during the year following admission in ICU. Secondary outcomes related to the mental health of participants during follow-up including hospital admission with a psychiatric disorder as the main or associated diagnosis, outpatient psychiatric consultation and psychotropic drugs prescription. Results At initial admission, patients in the transfer (n=319) and the control (n=794) groups were similar in age (64 years), sex (74% male), number of comorbidities and severity. However, transferred patients were lighter (- 8kg, p<0.001). Respectively 44 and 309 deaths were recorded in the transfer and control groups, the vast majority of which occurring while in ICU. At the end of follow-up, the adjusted incidence rate ratio associated with transfer was 0.18 (95% CI:0.13-0.24) thus suggesting a five-fold lower mortality risk. Transferred patients experienced twice as many psychiatric disorders during initial ICU stay (39.2% versus 18.3%, p<0.001) and these disorders were more often reported as associated (never as main) diagnosis of subsequent hospitalizations (28.8% versus 22%, p=0.04). However, both groups had similar rates of outpatient psychiatric consultations and prescriptions of psychotropic drugs during follow-up. Conclusions Mass extra-regional inter ICU transfers organised in France in spring 2020 were associated with both short- and long-term survival benefit. Mass-transfer to alleviate overcrowding should be considered an appropriate response to future sudden and localised increase in the demand for intensive care.

after.authors: Massey, J.; Hughes Kramer, K.; Snook Barrett, S.; Bishop, B.; Rothenberger, S.; Aslam, S.; Silveira, F.; Pilewski, J.; Robinson, K.; Zemke, A.; Shields, R. K.; Stellfox, M.; Van Tyne, D.; Haidar, G.
after.abstract:
BackgroundAchromobacter are a genus of difficult-to-treat, frequently multi-drug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria that can cause severe infections in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Bacteriophages are an understudied yet promising therapy for these and other antibiotic-resistant bacteria. However, data are largely limited to case reports or series, and clinical trials among pwCF to date have not evaluated Achromobacter.

MethodsThis is an investigator-initiated, open-label, randomized phase 1 pilot trial to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and biological effects of AchromoPhage, a cocktail of four genetically distinct, obligately lytic Achromobacter-targeting phages (phiACH01, phiACH04, phiACH06, phiACH07) with broad activity against Achromobacter species, in 12 adult participants with CF and pulmonary Achromobacter infection. Twelve participants will be randomized into three groups to receive a total of three, increasing, weekly doses of the AchromoPhage cocktail via one of three routes: 1) intravenous, 2) via inhalation, or 3) or intravenously and inhaled. Participation in the trial will span approximately 7 weeks, which will consist of outpatient phage dose administrations, safety and symptom monitoring, and longitudinal collection of biospecimens for protocol-specified and exploratory analyses through Day 42. The primary safety endpoint is the occurrence of treatment-related Grade 4 or greater adverse events. Secondary endpoints include longitudinal changes in FEV1 by spirometry, longitudinal changes in health-related quality of life, pharmacokinetics of each of the four phages in blood and the respiratory tract, and emergence of a phage neutralizing antibody response in serum.

DiscussionWhile existing case anecdotes and observational studies suggest that phages are safe and may have a role in treating human infections, there is a paucity of clinical trials studying the adverse effect profile and basic pharmacological parameters of phages. This trial will study the safety and explore the pharmacokinetic and other properties of a four-phage cocktail in patients with CF and chronic Achromobacter lung infection.

Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov NCT0727590. Registered on 12/10/2025

after.abstract:
BackgroundAchromobacter are a genus of difficult-to-treat, frequently multi-drug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria that can cause severe infections in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Bacteriophages are an understudied yet promising therapy for these and other antibiotic-resistant bacteria. However, data are largely limited to case reports or series, and clinical trials among pwCF to date have not evaluated Achromobacter.

MethodsThis is an investigator-initiated, open-label, randomized phase 1 pilot trial to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and biological effects of AchromoPhage, a cocktail of four genetically distinct, obligately lytic Achromobacter-targeting phages (phiACH01, phiACH04, phiACH06, phiACH07) with broad activity against Achromobacter species, in 12 adult participants with CF and pulmonary Achromobacter infection. Twelve participants will be randomized into three groups to receive a total of three, increasing, weekly doses of the AchromoPhage cocktail via one of three routes: 1) intravenous, 2) via inhalation, or 3) or intravenously and inhaled. Participation in the trial will span approximately 7 weeks, which will consist of outpatient phage dose administrations, safety and symptom monitoring, and longitudinal collection of biospecimens for protocol-specified and exploratory analyses through Day 42. The primary safety endpoint is the occurrence of treatment-related Grade 4 or greater adverse events. Secondary endpoints include longitudinal changes in FEV1 by spirometry, longitudinal changes in health-related quality of life, pharmacokinetics of each of the four phages in blood and the respiratory tract, and emergence of a phage neutralizing antibody response in serum.

DiscussionWhile existing case anecdotes and observational studies suggest that phages are safe and may have a role in treating human infections, there is a paucity of clinical trials studying the adverse effect profile and basic pharmacological parameters of phages. This trial will study the safety and explore the pharmacokinetic and other properties of a four-phage cocktail in patients with CF and chronic Achromobacter lung infection.

Trial registrationClinicalTrials.gov NCT0727590. Registered on 12/10/2025

after.title: Preprint: Direct tumour-adipocyte contact / Stroma AReactive Invasion Front Areas (TAC/SARIFA) in advanced oropharyngeal cancer
after.authors: Haas, S.; Maerkl, B.; Peiper, A.; Sauter, C.; Fiedler, L.; Ortmann, N.; Zenk, J.; Doescher, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: University Hospital Augsburg, department of ENT, head and neck surgery
after.abstract:
IntroductionStroma areactive invasion front areas (SARIFA) are a histopathological phenomenon at the tumour invasion front characterised by direct tumour-adipocyte contact (TAC). It can be detected on histological Haematoxylin-Eosin (H&E) stained tumour slides. TAC/SARIFA has emerged as a strong negative prognostic factor in several tumour entities. In this monocentric retrospective study, we aim to elucidate the impact of TAC/SARIFA in oropharyngeal cancer.

Materials and methods78 cases of pT3 - pT4 oropharyngeal squamous cell cancer from 2005 to 2023 and their corresponding lymph nodes were analysed for the occurrence of TAC/SARIFA. Besides, we compared overall survival rates, recurrence-free survival (RFS) and association with biological and pathological tumour characteristics.

ResultsIn total, overall survival was significantly reduced in TAC/SARIFA-positive tumours (p=0.014). Moreover, TAC/SARIFA-positive primary tumours are associated with TAC/SARIFA-positive lymph nodes (p<0.001) and extranodal extension (ENE) (p=0.032). Finally, RFS in TAC/SARIFA-positive tumours was reduced, but not significantly (p=0.072). No significant difference was found between p16-positive and p16-negative tumours and prevalence of TAC/SARIFA.

ConclusionTAC/SARIFA is a possible prognostically relevant risk factor in oropharyngeal cancer. When detected in the primary tumour or lymph nodes, it is associated with reduced overall survival rates and tendency towards shorter RFS. TAC/SARIFA-positive lymph nodes almost always show ENE.

after.title: Preprint: Association between Social Media Exposure and Self-Medication Practices: Public Health Implications in Punjab, Pakistan
after.authors: Ashraf, A.; Saddique, M. A. B.; Sajid, M. S.; Anjum, S.; Rizwan, F.; Qasim, M. Z.
after.abstract:
BackgroundSocial media has become an important source of health information, including information about medicines. Exposure to medicine-related content may affect decisions to use medicines without professional consultation.

ObjectiveTo describe self-medication practices and social-media exposure among adults in Punjab, Pakistan, and explore associations between self-medication frequency and demographic, social-media-use, and attitudinal factors. Methods: A cross-sectional analytical survey was conducted among adults aged 18-60 years in Punjab between March and May 2026. The final analytic sample comprised 280 participants. A bilingual (Urdu/English) questionnaire assessed demographics, social-media use and health-content exposure, self-medication in the preceding six months, medicine categories, and attitudes. The questionnaire was reviewed by two clinical experts and piloted among 30 participants. Descriptive analyses, chi-square tests, and multinomial logistic regression were reported using IBM SPSS Statistics; significance was set at =.05.

ResultsSelf-medication frequency was reported as Rarely by 117 participants (41.8%), Frequently by 130 (46.4%), and More Often by 33 (11.8%). Fever medicines were reported by 179 participants (63.9%) and gastrointestinal medicines by 96 (34.3%); multiple-response medicine categories were not mutually exclusive. Instagram was the most frequently selected social-media platform. Advertisement recall differed across self-medication frequency groups ({chi}2(22)=35.28, p=.036). Belief that medicines shown in advertisements/posts were safe was associated with self-medication frequency ({chi}2(4)=14.26, p=.007), while perceived risk was not ({chi}2(4)=1.587, p=.811). The multinomial models overall test was not statistically significant ({chi}2(40)=54.07, p=.068; Nagelkerke R2=.205). Likelihood-ratio tests identified associations for daily social-media-use duration ({chi}2(2)=13.085, p=.001), age group ({chi}2(6)=14.930, p=.021), and perceived advertisement safety ({chi}2(4)=10.899, p=.028).

ConclusionSelf-medication was commonly reported in this sample. Some social-media-use and advertising-attitude variables were associated with self-medication frequency, but the overall regression model was not statistically significant and the cross-sectional design cannot establish causality. Findings should be interpreted cautiously given the sample composition and reported data limitations.

Background: Achromobacter are a genus of difficult-to-treat, frequently multi-drug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria that can cause severe infections in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Bacteriophages are an understudied yet promising therapy for these and other antibiotic-resistant bacteria. However, data are largely limited to case reports or series, and clinical trials among pwCF to date have not evaluated Achromobacter.

Participation in the trial will span approximately 7 weeks, which will consist of outpatient phage dose administrations, safety and symptom monitoring, and longitudinal collection of biospecimens for protocol-specified and exploratory analyses through Day 42. Secondary endpoints include longitudinal changes in FEV1 by spirometry, longitudinal changes in health-related quality of life, pharmacokinetics of each of the four phages in blood and the respiratory tract, and emergence of a phage neutralizing antibody response in serum.

after.title: Preprint: Bladder scanning in children: accuracy of volume estimation and detection of urinary retention
after.authors: de Jong, A. C.; Arguedas Flores, O. E.; van Woensel, J. B. M.; Keunen, K.; Eijken, G. V.; de Kraker, T. M.; Maaskant, J. M.
after.abstract:
ObjectivesAccurate bladder volume assessment supports catheterization decisions in children, but evidence for the accuracy of automated bladder scanners is limited. In a large pediatric cohort, we assessed agreement between bladder scanner-estimated and catheterized volumes, and diagnostic accuracy for detecting urinary retention and elevated post-void residual (PVR).

Study designThis prospective cross-sectional study was conducted at a tertiary pediatric hospital. Children aged 0-12 years underwent bladder scanning (CUBEScan BioCon-900S) prior to clinically indicated catheterization or cystoscopy. Agreement was assessed using correlation and Bland-Altman analyses. Urinary retention (catheterized volume exceeding expected bladder capacity) and elevated PVR ([≥]4 years) were defined using age-specific thresholds.

ResultsIn 189 paired measurements from 181 children (median age 2.4 years), correlation was strong ({rho}=0.86). Despite a small mean difference (2 mL), 95% limits of agreement were wide (-91 to 95 mL), and only 38% of measurements were within {+/-}20% of catheterized volume. Agreement was moderate in children 2-12 years, and lowest in children <2 years and at volumes <100 mL. Overall specificity for urinary retention was 0.88, but sensitivity only 0.75, reflecting underestimation of elevated volumes, with an area under the curve of 0.75 overall versus 0.91 [≥]2 years. For elevated PVR, overall sensitivity was 0.98, but specificity 0.63.

ConclusionsBladder scanner-estimated volumes correlated well with catheterized volumes but showed limited agreement, particularly in children <2 years. This device is therefore not recommended in this age group. In older children, it may serve as an adjunct to clinical assessment of urinary retention.

after.abstract:
BackgroundNeurodegenerative disorders are common in ageing populations, and arise from several distinct pathophysiological causes. Yet, they also share many symptoms, including cognitive and neuropsychiatric ones. It is unclear to what extent the impact of neurodegeneration on brain systems is unique or shared across disorders, and whether shared symptoms are driven by degeneration of the same brain systems.

MethodsWe collected data from n=251 participants with Alzheimers Disease, Parkinsons Disease, Small Vessel Disease, and age-matched healthy controls. All participants underwent harmonized cognitive and neuropsychiatric assessment and were scanned using the UK-Biobank MRI protocol capturing features including brain volume, white matter lesions and microstructure, tract volume, iron content, and functional connectivity.

ResultsWe replicated established case-control brain changes in Alzheimers Disease, Parkinsons Disease and Small Vessel Disease compared to healthy controls. Leveraging this joint standardised dataset, we identified distinct neuroimaging features of individual neurodegenerative disorders, providing evidence for robust diagnosis-specific brain changes. Importantly, however, there was also a large degree of transdiagnostic similarity across neuroimaging markers. Testing for transdiagnostic associations between symptoms and brain phenotypes, we found that lower medial frontal pole connectivity to primary motor cortex was preferentially associated with apathy, fatigue, and depression; whereas cingulum microstructure was associated with cognitive deficits across diagnoses.

ConclusionsThese results demonstrate that different neurodegenerative diseases are characterised by dissociable brain changes, but also common transdiagnostic and symptom-associated features. This suggests that shared symptoms across neurodegeneration may in part be driven by overlapping impact on key brain systems, such as changes in medial frontal pole connectivity and cingulum microstructure. Our work highlights that multimodal imaging biomarkers can help understand and parse symptomatic heterogeneity in neurodegenerative and ageing populations.

after.abstract: Advances in ultrasensitive proteomics offer opportunities to characterize molecular pathways underlying brain aging. We measured 220 plasma proteins using NULISAseq Neuro220 in 250 Chinese, South Asian, and non-Hispanic White older adults (mean age=68.2 years; 70.4% female). Proteins implicated in neurodegenerative diseases (including brain-derived phosphorylated Tau; BDpTau), synaptic function, oxidative stress, and inflammation were associated with poorer cognition. Phosphorylated Tau205 was associated with reduced entorhinal thickness, whereas inflammatory proteins were associated with imaging markers of cerebral small vessel disease. Several findings were replicated in 1,381 participants in the Alzheimers Disease Neuroimaging Initiative, including associations of BDpTau species, NPTX2, BACE1, TREM1, CCL17, PRDX6, and IGF1R with cognitive decline and clinical progression. Cardiometabolic risk factors were associated with widespread proteomic alterations, many of which were also linked to poorer brain health. These results identify promising molecular markers of brain aging and extend proteomic research to ethnically diverse populations historically underrepresented in Alzheimers disease research.

after.abstract: Organ clocks estimate the biological age of organs from blood, but current clocks assign tissue-enriched proteins to organs and train on chronological age, which requires proteomics and does not yield organ-specific disease risk. In the UK Biobank, we trained organ clocks on first onset of disease of each organ using routine laboratory tests and froze the coefficients. Under an age label, organ-clock readouts arose equally in size-matched random protein panels; with a disease label, clocks selected their own organs proteins and predicted their own organs diseases. Defining extreme aging by multiples of disease risk concentrated flags on own-organ disease. Frozen clocks kept organ correspondence in the US NHANES cohort, predicted first onset of own-organ disease in the Japanese JMDC cohort and added more information to clinical risk scores than current organ clocks. Trained once where disease follow-up exists, organ clocks can be used wherever routine laboratory tests are measured.

after.authors: Balmaceda, C.; Rios Bustamante, J. C.; Lahoz, D.; Espinoza, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Centre for Research on Health and Social Care Management (CeRGAS), Bocconi University, Milan, Italy
after.abstract:
BackgroundChilean law requires a pharmacist to direct every pharmacy throughout opening hours. Bill 18,719-11 would allow any pharmacy to replace the pharmacist with another health professional or a technician, arguing that cheaper direction would open pharmacies where there are none and lower prices. We assessed that argument and the safety consequences.

MethodsWe built a societal-perspective simulation model comparing the bill with current regulation over 2027-2036. Pharmacist hours replaced determine the share of dispensings without a pharmacist, which drives additional adverse drug reactions and therapeutic-error poisonings, estimated from national hospital discharges and published data of the national poison centre. New access in municipalities without a pharmacy was valued. The increase in errors without a pharmacist and the share of harm originating in the affected pharmacies are unmeasured and were treated as scenarios. Labour-cost savings and the net health and access value were reported separately, discounted at 3%.

ResultsIn the reference scenario, 27% of dispensings would occur without a pharmacist by 2036. Over ten years the bill would add about 2,500 admissions for adverse drug reactions, 670 poisonings from therapeutic errors (28 of them admitted) and 68 deaths (95% interval 22-166). About 17,700 people would gain a pharmacy, worth CLP 12 billion (US$13 million), against CLP 150 billion (US$165 million) in health lost and care. The net health and access value was negative in 99.9% of simulations, and with any increase in errors above 3.2%. Pharmacies would save CLP 270 billion (US$296 million) in pay, lowering medicine spending by at most 0.6-1.9% if fully passed on. A favourable economic balance would require nearly three-quarters of displaced pharmacists to be re-employed immediately at the same pay.

ConclusionsThe access and price gains are small and local, whereas the health risks would be national. They do not justify allowing every pharmacy to replace its pharmacist; access in isolated localities calls for targeted measures.

after.abstract:
BackgroundResponsive feeding -- recognising and answering a childs hunger and satiety cues without coercion -- is a World Health Organization-recommended component of complementary feeding, yet it is rarely addressed or measured in Kenyas community health system, particularly in arid and semi-arid counties.

ObjectiveTo determine whether a Community Health Promoter (CHP)-led responsive feeding intervention improves responsive feeding practices among caregivers of children aged 0-59 months in West Pokot County, Kenya, compared with usual community health services, and to evaluate its implementation.

MethodsThis is a pragmatic, two-arm, parallel-group cluster randomized controlled trial with an embedded RE-AIM mixed-methods process evaluation. Eighteen Community Health Units in two sub-counties will be randomized 1:1, stratified by sub-county, and approximately 340 caregiver-child dyads enrolled. The intervention comprises five-day competency-based CHP training, monthly household counselling and coaching visits over three months, mother-to-mother group sessions, pictorial job aids, SMS reminders and supportive supervision with fidelity assessment. The comparator is usual care. The primary outcome is the Responsive Feeding Practices Index (RFPI, 0-100), combining observed mealtime and caregiver-reported items, at three months after intervention initiation. Secondary outcomes include caregiver knowledge, attitudes and self-efficacy, minimum dietary diversity, meal frequency and age-appropriate feeding. The primary analysis is a baseline-adjusted mixed-effects linear regression with a random intercept for Community Health Unit, by intention to treat. Reach, adoption, fidelity and maintenance, with key informant interviews and focus group discussions, will be integrated by RE-AIM domain.

Ethics and disseminationThe trial is approved by the Masinde Muliro University of Science and Technology Institutional Scientific and Ethics Review Committee (MMUST/ISERC/314/2026) and licensed by the National Commission for Science, Technology and Innovation (NACOSTI/P/26/4195285). Findings will be shared through publication, county feedback meetings and a policy brief.

Trial registrationPan African Clinical Trials Registry, PACTR202611787801603; registered 9 November 2026; enrolment planned from 11 January 2027.

after.authors: Clumeck, S.; Rojas, C. R.; Kowuor, D.; Sesay, H. S.; Ameh, S.; Galarraga, O.; Ogbuanu, I. U.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The Africa Research Collaborative (The ARC), on behalf of the Child Health and Mortality Prevention Surveillance
after.abstract:
AO_SCPLOWBSTRACTC_SCPLOWO_ST_ABSObjectiveC_ST_ABSDeveloping equitable prevention of mother-to-child transmission (PMTCT) policies requires local evidence, yet how socioeconomic, geographic, and health system factors jointly drive HIV-related child mortality remains underexplored in Sierra Leone. This study evaluated the association between socioeconomic status (SES), geographic access, and pediatric HIV-related mortality, while examining the system-level and sociocultural barriers driving missed PMTCT opportunities.

Materials and MethodsWe used a mixed-methods design. Quantitative analyses drew on Child Health and Mortality Prevention Surveillance Sierra Leone surveillance data (2019-2024) for deceased under five years old (U5s) with confirmed HIV status. Stepwise logistic regression evaluated associations between covariates (SES, maternal education, distance to health facilities) and a composite binary outcome of HIV-related death. Qualitatively, 33 key informant interviews with PMTCT stakeholders were analyzed using thematic framework analysis in Dedoose.

ResultsThe quantitative sample included 1,230 deceased children, of whom 162 (13.2%) reported an HIV-related death. Maternal education and distance to health facilities were statistically significant predictors of HIV-related death, whereas wealth quintiles showed no association. The qualitative findings identified system-level constraints disrupting the PMTCT cascade, including delayed entry into antenatal care, weak postnatal follow-up, stockouts of HIV test kits and antiretroviral drugs, limited polymerase chain reaction capacity and delayed results, and gaps in scheduling, tracking, and data systems. Donor-driven targets and funding constraints shaped procurement and service availability. Stigma, fear of disclosure, confidentiality concerns, transport costs, and poverty further undermined engagement and retention.

ConclusionsPediatric HIV infection and related outcomes were driven by cumulative barriers across access, service readiness, and sociocultural context rather than household wealth alone. Improving PMTCT outcomes requires strengthening diagnostic and supply chain infrastructure, enhancing patient-tracking systems, and delivering stigma-sensitive, community-anchored care.

Quantitative analyses drew on Child Health and Mortality Prevention Surveillance Sierra Leone surveillance data (2019-2024) for deceased under five years old (U5s) with confirmed HIV status. Stepwise logistic regression evaluated associations between covariates (SES, maternal education, distance to health facilities) and a composite binary outcome of HIV-related death. Qualitatively, 33 key informant interviews with PMTCT stakeholders were analyzed using thematic framework analysis in Dedoose.

ResultsThe quantitative sample included 1,230 deceased children, of whom 162 (13.2%) reported an HIV-related death. Maternal education and distance to health facilities were statistically significant predictors of HIV-related death, whereas wealth quintiles showed no association. The qualitative findings identified system-level constraints disrupting the PMTCT cascade, including delayed entry into antenatal care, weak postnatal follow-up, stockouts of HIV test kits and antiretroviral drugs, limited polymerase chain reaction capacity and delayed results, and gaps in scheduling, tracking, and data systems. Donor-driven targets and funding constraints shaped procurement and service availability. Stigma, fear of disclosure, confidentiality concerns, transport costs, and poverty further undermined engagement and retention.

ConclusionsPediatric HIV infection and related outcomes were driven by cumulative barriers across access, service readiness, and sociocultural context rather than household wealth alone. Improving PMTCT outcomes requires strengthening diagnostic and supply chain infrastructure, enhancing patient-tracking systems, and delivering stigma-sensitive, community-anchored care.

C_LI

Funding, acknowledgements, conflicts of interest and author contributions are given in the Declarations section.

after.title: Preprint: Direct RNA sequencing reveals an m6A downregulated on APOEϵ4 RNA in brain from Alzheimer's disease cases and controls
after.authors: Fox, G. A.; Page, M. L.; Wadsworth, M. E.; Heberle, B. A.; Gordon, L. A.; Fardo, D. W.; Johnson, L. A.; Beach, T. G.; Serrano, G. E.; Nelson, P. T.; Ebbert, M. T. W.
after.abstract: APOE harbors the strongest common genetic risk factors for late-onset Alzheimer's disease (AD), yet its disease mechanism remains incompletely understood. Two missense SNPs jointly define the APOE alleles, with rs429358 distinguishing {epsilon}4 from {epsilon}3, but whether other APOE features, such as mRNA modifications, contribute to APOE-associated AD risk is unknown. Here, we performed deep long-read direct RNA sequencing on human frontal cortex from six AD cases and six controls to characterize native mRNA modifications transcriptome-wide and across AD-relevant genes. We evaluated differential nucleotide modifications between cases and controls transcriptome-wide, and we then performed two association tests within APOE: (1) associations between mRNA modifications and rs429358 alleles in five {epsilon}3/{epsilon}4 heterozygotes; and (2) pairwise associations between co-occurring mRNA modifications. We identified four modifications associated with rs429358--all within 15 nucleotides of the SNP. Among them was an N6-methyladenosine (m6A) located at chr19:44,908,679 (OR = 0.53; p = 1.4x10-109)--five nucleotides upstream of rs429358--that was 14.5 percentage points lower on {epsilon}4-derived mRNA (27.7%) compared to {epsilon}3 (42.2%). This directional difference was observed within each individual, supporting a consistent allele-associated modification pattern (p = 4.2x10-5). We also identified 344 associations among 73 APOE modifications, suggesting a potentially complex, coordinated network of mRNA biological signals within APOE, alone. Our findings suggest that mRNA modifications may contribute to APOE-associated risk, though validation in large independent cohorts and functional experiments will be necessary to determine the biological consequences of these associations and their potential relevance to AD pathogenesis. Together, our findings highlight the potential of allele-resolved direct RNA sequencing to characterize genetic associations with RNA modifications at a major AD risk locus.

after.title: Preprint: Integrated Stepped-Care Task-Shared Intervention for Depression Symptoms in Older Adults Living with HIV in Nigeria: A pilot randomized controlled study
after.authors: Elugbadebo, O. O.; Akintade, F. M.; Omoloye, T. T.; Oladeji, B. D.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Department of Psychiatry, College of Medicine, University of Ibadan, Oyo
after.abstract: **Background** Depression can affect treatment adherence and quality of life of older adults living with HIV, yet evidence on integrated stepped-care task-shared (SCT) interventions in African settings remains limited. We assessed the feasibility of an adapted SCT intervention among adults aged >=50 years receiving HIV care in Ibadan, Nigeria and examined preliminary differences in depressive symptoms, quality of life and ART adherence. **Methods** This was a two-arm, parallel-group, randomised pilot superiority trial embedded in a mixed-methods effectiveness-implementation study in Ibadan, Nigeria. Adults aged >=50 years living with HIV and scoring >=10 on the Patient Health Questionnaire-9 (PHQ-9) were randomised (1:1) to stepped-care task-sharing (SCT; n=50) or treatment as usual (TAU; n=50). SCT involved psychosocial sessions delivered by trained HIV clinic providers, with antidepressant treatment and specialist review according to depression severity and treatment response. TAU involved routine HIV care and referral to a separate psychiatric clinic. Outcomes were assessed at six weeks, three months and six months by assessors blinded to allocation. Feasibility indicators included recruitment, retention and intervention delivery. Preliminary clinical effectiveness was assessed using mixed-effects models for PHQ-9, quality of life (WHOQOL-HIV BREF) and ART adherence (Simplified Medication Adherence Questionnaire). Analyses followed randomised allocation using Stata/MP 15. The trial was registered with ClinicalTrials.gov (NCT06894680). **Results** Of the 757 participants screened, 120 participants were eligible and 100 (83.3%) were randomised, with 50 allocated to the SCT and 50 to TAU. All 50 SCT participants received the first psychosocial session, 40 (80%) attended at least two sessions and 30 (60%) completed all six sessions. Of 23 participants prescribed antidepressants, five (21.7%) initiated treatment. Baseline mean PHQ-9 scores were 13.24 (SD 4.43) in SCT and 14.12 (SD 4.48) in TAU. Of the 17 participants in TAU referred to the UCH psychiatric clinic, one attended but subsequently disengaged from care. Adjusted between-group differences (TAU minus SCT) favoured SCT at six weeks (3.95 points, 95% CI 1.91-5.99; p<0.001), three months (3.66, 95% CI 1.60-5.71; p<0.001) and six months (3.15, 95% CI 1.09-5.20; p=0.003). Quality-of-life scores increased in both groups, with no significant between-group differences at baseline, 3 months, or 6 months (all p>0.05). Differences in quality of life and ART adherence were not statistically significant. No adverse events were recorded. **Conclusion** This pilot trial demonstrated that the recruitment, retention and psychosocial SCT delivery were feasible within routine HIV care. SCT showed promising reductions in depressive symptoms over six months, although antidepressant initiation was limited. Further multisite evaluation should examine clinical effectiveness, intervention fidelity and implementation outcomes.

after.authors: Zhang, M.; Song, X.; Pan, Z.; Wan, M.; Song, Z.; Li, J.
after.author_corresponding_institution: The First Affiliated Hospital of Army Medical University (Southwest Hospital)
after.abstract: Background: Persistent facial erythema and episodic flushing are prominent features of erythematotelangiectatic rosacea (ETR). The efficacy of auricular acupuncture (AA) for ETR is uncertain. Methods: This multicenter, randomized, participant- and assessor-masked, sham-controlled superiority trial was designed to enroll 108 adults aged 18 to 50 years with ETR and a baseline Clinician Erythema Assessment (CEA) score of at least 2 at 5 hospitals in China. Participants were allocated 1:1 to AA with semipermanent intradermal needles or visually matched, same-site nonpenetrating sham stimulation. Four auricular points (Shenmen, Sanjiao, Endocrine, and Heart) were treated on alternating ears every 3 days for 6 weeks, with self-pressure 3 times daily. Follow-up was scheduled through week 10. The primary outcome was clinician-rated erythema (CEA score) at week 6. Secondary outcomes comprised other clinician-rated erythema assessments, patient-rated redness, flushing, migraine symptoms, sleep quality, depressive and anxiety symptoms, and adverse events. The primary treatment contrast was planned using baseline-adjusted analysis of covariance with multiple imputation for missing week 6 outcomes. Secondary longitudinal outcomes were planned for exploratory mixed-model analyses. Discussion: The trial was designed to assess the incremental efficacy and tolerability of penetrating auricular needling compared with a matched nonpenetrating procedure. Same-site pressure in both groups may have physiological effects, which should be considered when interpreting the results.

after.abstract: Organ clocks estimate the biological age of organs from blood, but current clocks assign tissue-enriched proteins to organs and train on chronological age, which requires proteomics and does not yield organ-specific disease risk. In the UK Biobank, we trained organ clocks on first onset of disease of each organ using routine laboratory tests and froze the coefficients. Under an age label, organ-clock readouts arose equally in size-matched random protein panels; with a disease label, clocks selected their own organ's proteins and predicted their own organ's diseases. Defining extreme aging by multiples of disease risk concentrated flags on own-organ disease. Frozen clocks kept organ correspondence in the US NHANES cohort, predicted first onset of own-organ disease in the Japanese JMDC cohort and added more information to clinical risk scores than current organ clocks. Trained once where disease follow-up exists, organ clocks can be used wherever routine laboratory tests are measured.

after.authors: Balmaceda, C.; Rios Bustamante, J. C.; Lahoz, D.; Espinoza, M.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Centre for Research on Health and Social Care Management (CeRGAS), Bocconi University, Milan, Italy
after.abstract: Background Chilean law requires a pharmacist to direct every pharmacy throughout opening hours. Bill 18,719-11 would allow any pharmacy to replace the pharmacist with another health professional or a technician, arguing that cheaper direction would open pharmacies where there are none and lower prices. We assessed that argument and the safety consequences. Methods We built a societal-perspective simulation model comparing the bill with current regulation over 2027-2036. Pharmacist hours replaced determine the share of dispensings without a pharmacist, which drives additional adverse drug reactions and therapeutic-error poisonings, estimated from national hospital discharges and published data of the national poison centre. New access in municipalities without a pharmacy was valued. The increase in errors without a pharmacist and the share of harm originating in the affected pharmacies are unmeasured and were treated as scenarios. Labour-cost savings and the net health and access value were reported separately, discounted at 3%. Results In the reference scenario, 27% of dispensings would occur without a pharmacist by 2036. Over ten years the bill would add about 2,500 admissions for adverse drug reactions, 670 poisonings from therapeutic errors (28 of them admitted) and 68 deaths (95% interval 22-166). About 17,700 people would gain a pharmacy, worth CLP 12 billion (US$13 million), against CLP 150 billion (US$165 million) in health lost and care. The net health and access value was negative in 99.9% of simulations, and with any increase in errors above 3.2%. Pharmacies would save CLP 270 billion (US$296 million) in pay, lowering medicine spending by at most 0.6-1.9% if fully passed on. A favourable economic balance would require nearly three-quarters of displaced pharmacists to be re-employed immediately at the same pay. Conclusions The access and price gains are small and local, whereas the health risks would be national. They do not justify allowing every pharmacy to replace its pharmacist; access in isolated localities calls for targeted measures.

after.title: Preprint: Rapid species-specific molecular diagnosis of amoebic liver abscess by isothermal RNA amplification: a case report
after.authors: Pereira Neves, H.; Dias Guimaraes, A. R.; Leao dos Santos, J. F.; Martins Magnus, M.; Ribeiro Silva, V.; Bandeira da Silva, R.; Sobreira Messias, G.; Ferreira, W. E.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Rene Rachou Institute, Oswaldo Cruz Foundation; Lucas Machado Educational Foundation
after.abstract: Background Amoebic liver abscess, caused by Entamoeba histolytica, is a potential life threatening extra intestinal infection that is prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions. Entamoeba histolytica is morphologically indistinguishable from the non-pathogenic Entamoeba dispar, yet species-level confirmation is critical before initiating metronidazole. This is particularly important in elderly patients, for whom the drug carries a higher risk of QT prolongation, peripheral neuropathy, and hepatotoxicity. In Brazil, where E. dispar predominates over E. histolytica at an estimated 10:1 ratio, diagnostic misidentification constitutes a genuine hazard. Methodology and Principal Findings We report a patient with amoebic liver abscess with secondary hepatic biochemical derangement requiring urgent molecular species confirmation. A Nucleic Acid Sequence- Based Amplification (NASBA) assay was designed targeting a species-specific region of the E. histolytica 40S small subunit ribosomal RNA (GenBank MW026793.1). Primer design using NCBI Primer-BLAST yielded a thermodynamically balanced primer pair, with melting temperatures of 53.25{degrees}C and 53.81{degrees}C and a resulting amplicon with 121 nucleotides, which is suitable for standard NASBA at 41{degrees}C. Applied to an aspirated abscess sample, the assay returned a positive result confirming E. histolytica infection and enabling continuation of antiamoebic therapy with favourable clinical outcome. Conclusions and Significance NASBA targeting E. histolytica small subunit ribosomal RNA provides species-specific diagnosis through two orthogonal mechanisms: sequence-level discrimination from E. dispar at the primer binding sites, and the intrinsic viability bias or RNA amplification, which favours signal from metabolically active trophozoites over residual nucleic acid. The episomal architecture of E. histolytica ribosomal DNA, which has approximately 200 extrachromosomal gene copies per trophozoite (each actively transcribed), confers inherent sensitivity amplification. Operating isothermally at 41{degrees}C without a thermocycler or any additional laboratory infrastructure, this approach addresses a genuine diagnostic gap in neglected tropical disease management and is suited to point-of-care deployment in resource-limited endemic settings.

after.abstract: Background: Achromobacter are a genus of difficult-to-treat, frequently multi-drug-resistant Gram-negative bacteria that can cause severe infections in people with cystic fibrosis (pwCF). Bacteriophages are an understudied yet promising therapy for these and other antibiotic-resistant bacteria. However, data are largely limited to case reports or series, and clinical trials among pwCF to date have not evaluated Achromobacter. Methods: This is an investigator-initiated, open-label, randomized phase 1 pilot trial to evaluate the safety, tolerability, and biological effects of AchromoPhage, a cocktail of four genetically distinct, obligately lytic Achromobacter-targeting phages (phiACH01, phiACH04, phiACH06, phiACH07) with broad activity against Achromobacter species, in 12 adult participants with CF and pulmonary Achromobacter infection. Twelve participants will be randomized into three groups to receive a total of three, increasing, weekly doses of the AchromoPhage cocktail via one of three routes: 1) intravenous, 2) via inhalation, or 3) or intravenously and inhaled. Participation in the trial will span approximately 7 weeks, which will consist of outpatient phage dose administrations, safety and symptom monitoring, and longitudinal collection of biospecimens for protocol-specified and exploratory analyses through Day 42. The primary safety endpoint is the occurrence of treatment-related Grade 4 or greater adverse events. Secondary endpoints include longitudinal changes in FEV1 by spirometry, longitudinal changes in health-related quality of life, pharmacokinetics of each of the four phages in blood and the respiratory tract, and emergence of a phage neutralizing antibody response in serum. Discussion: While existing case anecdotes and observational studies suggest that phages are safe and may have a role in treating human infections, there is a paucity of clinical trials studying the adverse effect profile and basic pharmacological parameters of phages. This trial will study the safety and explore the pharmacokinetic and other properties of a four-phage cocktail in patients with CF and chronic Achromobacter lung infection. Trial registration: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT0727590. Registered on 12/10/2025

after.authors: Theberge, E. T.; Anderson, S. J.; Lehman, A. M.
after.abstract: Purpose: Diagnostic yield from genetic testing in cardiomyopathy depends on reference data and access to care, which differ by race and gender, yet are rarely studied jointly. Methods: We analyzed 414,830 genome-sequenced All of Us participants for predicted deleterious variants (PDVs) in 58 cardiomyopathy genes, comparing ClinVar classifications by race and modelling cardiac outcomes against matched controls and, within heterozygotes, by race and gender. Among GLA or TTR pathogenic/likely pathogenic (P/LP) carriers with cardiomyopathy, we explored Fabry disease or amyloidosis diagnosis codes by race, gender, income and education. Results: PDVs in White participants were more often P/LP (13.9% vs 12.0%, p<0.001), more so among heterozygotes with cardiomyopathy (29.6% vs 22.1%, p=0.004). Cardiomyopathy odds rose from missense to loss-of-function PDVs (OR 1.12-1.79). Twenty of 131 GLA/TTR P/LP carriers with cardiomyopathy had a syndromic code; White women had higher odds than non-White women (OR 6.50, 95% CI 1.35-31.34). Syndromic codes were nominally associated with higher income and education, and 47 of 48 carriers with income <$25k were non-White. Conclusion: Variant classification and syndromic diagnosis are less complete for non-White carriers, particularly women. Equitable precision cardiology requires more diverse reference data and analyses that treat race and gender as effect modifiers.

after.authors: Khoury, L.; Osakwe, A.; Martinez-Jaramillo, E.; Vu, D.; Rajaram, A.; Alqahtani, A.; Chergui, M.; Osman, M.; Lefrancois, P.; Xu, L.; Li, Y.; Netchiporouk, E.
after.abstract: Background: Localized scleroderma (LS, morphea) is an immune-mediated fibrosing skin disease whose molecular basis in adults, and its variation with clinical activity and histological stage, are poorly defined. Objectives: To characterize transcriptional, cellular and senescence-associated programs in adult LS by clinical activity, histological stage and subtype, and to compare them with those of other inflammatory skin diseases. Methods: We performed bulk RNA sequencing of archival lesional skin from 60 adults with LS and 22 healthy controls (HC), with enrichment analyses, cell-type deconvolution, immune-module scoring, cross-disease comparison and p16INK4a immunohistochemistry. Results: LS lesions showed 704 differentially expressed genes versus HC, enriched for interferon signaling, antigen presentation and T-helper differentiation pathways; changes were extensive in clinically active (n = 49) and histologically inflammatory (n = 21) lesions but limited in fibrotic lesions (n = 33). Deconvolution inferred expansion of fibroblasts, macrophages and regulatory, cytotoxic and helper T cells, with co-expression of effector and checkpoint genes in T-cell profiles (IFNG, GZMK, LAG3, TIGIT). Th1 and Th17 activity was higher in inflammatory than in fibrotic lesions, whereas Th2 activity did not differ between them. A senescence-associated gene set was enriched in LS (normalized enrichment score 1.64), including fibrotic lesions (nominal P <0.05), and dermal p16INK4a-positive cell density was higher than in HC (median 113.9 vs 36.0 cells/mm^2; P = 0.003). LS signatures most closely resembled those of cutaneous lupus erythematosus and lichen planus. Conclusions: Adult LS shows interferon-associated T-cell activation, most pronounced in clinically active and histologically inflammatory disease, and a senescence-associated signature. Type-2 and senescence-associated programs persist in fibrotic lesions. These findings support Janus kinase-signal transducer and activator of transcription (JAK-STAT) inhibition in active disease and trials of senescence-modulating therapies across disease stages.

after.authors: Ntirenganya, F.; Ishema, L.; Ndayisenga, F.; El-Khatib, Z.; Zinsstag, J.; Rwagasore, E.
after.abstract: Background Rift Valley fever recurred in Rwanda in 2018, 2022, 2025 and 2026 despite yearly livestock vaccination. Vaccines protect best if given before transmission speeds up, but the deadline for vaccination and the sectors to prioritise have not been estimated. We aimed to estimate the latest dates to start and finish a campaign and to identify priority sectors. Methodology We analysed surveillance data from four outbreaks: 1,090 animals and 416 laboratory-confirmed people in 2026, plus 2022, 2025 and 2018 data, vegetation and rainfall records. A negative binomial regression of weekly livestock cases gave the growth rate, the basic reproduction number and the start of transmission. We simulated the latest campaign dates 100,000 times, allowing for delays to immunity and campaigns. We ranked 416 sectors using pre-2026 information, tested by leaving out each district in turn. Livestock cases doubled every 9.3 days (95% confidence interval 8.1-10.8) and the basic reproduction number was 1.78 (1.64-1.92); assuming 90% vaccine efficacy, 48.5% coverage (43.4-53.3) was needed to stop spread. For the earliest outbreak (March 2022), live-attenuated vaccine had to start by 11 January (24 December-28 January) and finish by 22 February (11 February-3 March). A campaign begun at first detection would have protected animals after 220 of 1,090 livestock cases (20%) and 149 of 416 human cases (36%) had occurred. Sectors ranked before the season, mainly by the districts 2022 attack rate, that held 25% of animals contained 66% of livestock cases and 86% of human cases (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.73). Conclusions Waiting until an outbreak is detected is too late to prevent many early cases, so campaigns should be planned around the earliest-starting outbreak, with a later round to protect animals through the year. Districts and sectors with earlier outbreaks should be prioritised.

after.title: Preprint: Sources of protein in UK adults following contemporary plant-based diets: findings from the Feeding the Future (FEED) Study
after.authors: Lawson, I.; Bell, W.; Key, T. J.; Papier, K.
after.abstract: Objective To identify and quantify sources of protein intake in United Kingdom (UK) adults following different diets, and assess how these sources contribute to meeting protein requirements. Design Cross-sectional analysis of the Feeding the Future Study (FEED), a UK cohort recruited in 2022-2023. Dietary intake was assessed using an online food frequency questionnaire. We calculated the percentage contribution of food groups to daily protein intake, and the proportion of participants meeting the estimated average requirement (EAR) for protein, with and without exclusion of under-reporters. Setting A contemporary cohort of UK adults. Participants 6,113 adults: 1,540 omnivores, 1,322 flexitarians, 547 pescatarians, 1,212 vegetarians, and 1,492 vegans. Results Grains contributed 10-30% of total protein intake across all groups. Dairy contributed 12.9-14.2% in non-vegan groups, while plant-based dairy alternatives contributed less in vegans (7%), mainly from soy milk (4.3%). Other major contributors (>10%) were meat for omnivores (33.0%) and flexitarians (13.5%); fish for pescatarians (14.9%); plant-based meat alternatives for vegetarians (12.0%); and plant-based meat alternatives (15.0%), legumes and pulses (10.5%), and nuts and seeds (10.5%) for vegans. The proportion below the protein EAR ranged from 1.9% in omnivores to 14.0% in vegans, falling to 0.01% and 3.6% respectively, after excluding under-reporters. Conclusions Grains were a major contributor to protein intake across all diet groups, as was dairy in all non-vegan groups. Protein sources were more varied in non-omnivorous groups, particularly vegans. Few participants fell below the protein EAR and the higher proportions among vegetarians and vegans were largely attenuated after excluding under-reporters.

data.summary: added: Preprint: Bladder scanning in children: accuracy of volume estimation and detection of urinary retention

after.title: Preprint: Bladder scanning in children: accuracy of volume estimation and detection of urinary retention
after.authors: de Jong, A. C.; Arguedas Flores, O. E.; van Woensel, J. B. M.; Keunen, K.; Eijken, G. V.; de Kraker, T. M.; Maaskant, J. M.
after.abstract: Objectives Accurate bladder volume assessment supports catheterization decisions in children, but evidence for the accuracy of automated bladder scanners is limited. In a large pediatric cohort, we assessed agreement between bladder scanner-estimated and catheterized volumes, and diagnostic accuracy for detecting urinary retention and elevated post-void residual (PVR). Study design This prospective cross-sectional study was conducted at a tertiary pediatric hospital. Children aged 0-12 years underwent bladder scanning (CUBEScan BioCon-900S) prior to clinically indicated catheterization or cystoscopy. Agreement was assessed using correlation and Bland-Altman analyses. Urinary retention (catheterized volume exceeding expected bladder capacity) and elevated PVR ([≥] 4 years) were defined using age-specific thresholds. Results In 189 paired measurements from 181 children (median age 2.4 years), correlation was strong ({rho}=0.86). Despite a small mean difference (2 mL), 95% limits of agreement were wide (-91 to 95 mL), and only 38% of measurements were within {+/-}20% of catheterized volume. Agreement was moderate in children 2-12 years, and lowest in children <2 years and at volumes <100 mL. Overall specificity for urinary retention was 0.88, but sensitivity only 0.75, reflecting underestimation of elevated volumes, with an area under the curve of 0.75 overall versus 0.91 [≥]2 years. For elevated PVR, overall sensitivity was 0.98, but specificity 0.63. Conclusions Bladder scanner-estimated volumes correlated well with catheterized volumes but showed limited agreement, particularly in children <2 years. This device is therefore not recommended in this age group. In older children, it may serve as an adjunct to clinical assessment of urinary retention.

data.summary: added: Preprint: Procedure composition, age and race/color in gender-affirming surgical authorizations of the Brazilian public health system, 2014-2025

after.title: Preprint: Procedure composition, age and race/color in gender-affirming surgical authorizations of the Brazilian public health system, 2014-2025
after.authors: dos Santos, J.; Amorim Costa, C. M.
after.abstract: Hospital admission authorizations from publicly financed health systems are increasingly used to describe gender-affirming surgery, although they record billed procedures whose feminizing or masculinizing direction can be inferred from the code, without identifying people, self-reported gender identity or clinical need. This nationwide descriptive study examined the authorizations for gender-affirming surgery processed by the Brazilian Unified Health System from 2014 to 2025, which were selected from 3,888 public monthly state files of the Hospital Information System with a historically versioned classification of procedure codes. Of the 1,375 selected authorizations, 711 corresponded to directly feminizing procedures, 428 to directly masculinizing procedures and 236 to a complementary procedure that was analyzed separately. The feminizing share of the directly classified authorizations decreased from 81.7% (196/240) in 2014-2018 to 72.2% (213/295) in 2019-2023 and to 50.0% (302/604) in 2024-2025, proportions that describe composition within periods of unequal length and cannot be read as population rates. In 2024-2025, bilateral mastectomy accounted for 264 of the 302 masculinizing authorizations (87.4%), whereas bilateral breast reconstruction with silicone implants accounted for 118 of the 302 feminizing authorizations (39.1%). The median recorded age was 35 years in feminizing and 30 years in masculinizing authorizations over the whole period, and 34 and 29 years when the comparison was restricted to 2024-2025. The brown (parda) race/color category was recorded in 42.6% (303/711) of feminizing and 61.0% (261/428) of masculinizing authorizations, in a comparison pooled over the whole period and not adjusted for period or procedure. The number of hospitals habilitated for these surgeries remained at five from 2014 to 2022 and doubled in 2023. All aggregate results were reproduced by an independent pipeline that re-read every original public file. It was observed that the equal numbers of feminizing and masculinizing authorizations in the most recent period resulted from markedly different procedure portfolios, which suggests that the monitoring of publicly funded gender-affirming surgery may benefit from procedure-specific indicators and versioned code definitions, while questions of access and equity would require person-level and patient-reported data.

after.title: Preprint: Community Health Promoter-led responsive feeding for caregivers of children aged 0-59 months in West Pokot, Kenya (CHP-RF-WP Trial): protocol for a pragmatic cluster randomized controlled trial with mixed-methods evaluation
after.authors: Koross, A. K.; Morema, E. N.; Konyole, S. O.; Shisanya, M. S.
after.abstract: Background. Responsive feeding -- recognising and answering a childs hunger and satiety cues without coercion -- is a World Health Organization-recommended component of complementary feeding, yet it is rarely addressed or measured in Kenyas community health system, particularly in arid and semi-arid counties. Objective. To determine whether a Community Health Promoter (CHP)-led responsive feeding intervention improves responsive feeding practices among caregivers of children aged 0-59 months in West Pokot County, Kenya, compared with usual community health services, and to evaluate its implementation. Methods. This is a pragmatic, two-arm, parallel-group cluster randomized controlled trial with an embedded RE-AIM mixed-methods process evaluation. Eighteen Community Health Units in two sub-counties will be randomized 1:1, stratified by sub-county, and approximately 340 caregiver-child dyads enrolled. The intervention comprises five-day competency-based CHP training, monthly household counselling and coaching visits over three months, mother-to-mother group sessions, pictorial job aids, SMS reminders and supportive supervision with fidelity assessment. The comparator is usual care. The primary outcome is the Responsive Feeding Practices Index (RFPI, 0-100), combining observed mealtime and caregiver-reported items, at three months after intervention initiation. Secondary outcomes include caregiver knowledge, attitudes and self-efficacy, minimum dietary diversity, meal frequency and age-appropriate feeding. The primary analysis is a baseline-adjusted mixed-effects linear regression with a random intercept for Community Health Unit, by intention to treat. Reach, adoption, fidelity and maintenance, with key informant interviews and focus group discussions, will be integrated by RE-AIM domain. Ethics and dissemination. The trial is approved by the Masinde Muliro University of Science and Technology Institutional Scientific and Ethics Review Committee (MMUST/ISERC/314/2026) and licensed by the National Commission for Science, Technology and Innovation (NACOSTI/P/26/4195285). Findings will be shared through publication, county feedback meetings and a policy brief. Trial registration. Pan African Clinical Trials Registry, PACTR202611787801603; registered 9 November 2026; enrolment planned from 11 January 2027.

after.authors: Jain, P.; Bolas, T.; Nabia, S.; Agarwal, A.; Malik, C.; Tripathi, A.; Sharma, S.; Bansal, P.; Agarwal, A.; Jain, A.; Malhotra, A.; Khan, R.; Chowdhury, A.; Mukherjee, P. S.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Cambridge Health Alliance; The Frontline Knowledge Project
after.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) perform well on physician reasoning tasks, sparking interest in using them to guide mid-level health providers where physicians are scarce. However, evidence is lacking for effective LLM interfaces and their performance in real patient encounters. We report the human-centered design and performance of the NurseAI mobile app in rural West Bengal, India. Nurses participated in six design rounds that culminated in an audio-based mobile app that listens to the patient interview in the patients native language, suggests patient-specific questions for the nurse, and generates an assessment and plan. Physician graders evaluated the apps output for fifty real-patient consultations in the final version and found 90% of the plans were appropriate, 96% valid, and 94% safe. Several feature improvements have been identified for future versions of the app from the field use.

after.title: Preprint: Interrater Reliability of Clinical Resting-State fMRI Network Classification: Comparison of Human Raters and an AI Algorithm
after.authors: Kang, A. B.; Reuther, W. R.; Robinson, B.; Kazemi, M. H.; Boerwinkle, V. L.
after.author_corresponding_institution: Division of Child Neurology, University of North Carolina School of Medicine, Chapel Hill, North Carolina, United States of America
after.abstract: Purpose Accurate classification of intrinsic brain networks is essential for the clinical interpretation of resting-state functional MRI (rs-fMRI), especially in complex pediatric populations. Manual classification of resting-state networks (RSNs) remains the clinical gold standard, yet variability among raters poses a challenge for reproducibility. This study aims to assess interrater reliability among five human raters and one AI algorithm. Methods Rs-fMRI data were collected from 269 scans in a clinical cohort predominantly composed of pediatric patients. Raters used an independent component analysis (ICA)-based pipeline to categorize RSNs into one of 13 categories. Percent agreement, Cohen's Kappa, and Fleiss's Kappa were used to measure agreement. Results Overall pairwise agreement for human-human pairs ranged from substantial to almost perfect ({kappa} = 0.655-0.845), while human-AI agreement ranged from fair to moderate ({kappa} = 0.289-0.401). Agreement was highest for Typical networks and Noise, whereas Atypical networks showed lower agreement, with moderate human-human agreement ({kappa} = 0.468-0.541) and poor-to-fair human-AI agreement ({kappa} = 0.147-0.305). Despite high human-human agreement on Noise components, human-AI kappa values for Noise were disproportionately low, a pattern that may reflect the high prevalence of Noise components and class imbalance in the model's training data. Conclusion Our findings underscore the need for standardized classification frameworks and targeted training to improve consistency, particularly for atypical networks. This study supports the development of reproducible rs-fMRI workflows and the potential use of AI as a complementary screening tool within clinical neuroimaging workflows.

after.title: Preprint: Impact of Artificial Intelligence Assistance on Efficiency, Ergonomics, and Measurement Consistency of Abdominal Ultrasound
after.authors: Barr, R. G.; Gao, J.; Lim, A.; Neill, B.
after.abstract: OObjectives: Evaluate how the addition of AI-assisted image acquisition and measurements affects the efficiency, ergonomics, accuracy, and consistency of abdominal ultrasound examination. Methods: Randomized, crossover study utilizing an abdominal ultrasound system with integrated AI features. Experienced sonographers (N=33) performed standardized examinations with and without AI-assisted features enabled. Metrics of timing and control interactions by the non-scanning hand were acquired. Movements of the non-scanning hand were recorded during a subset of examinations (N=17) to evaluate distance traveled with and without AI. An offline measurement exercise (N=32) using standardized image datasets assessed agreement between AI-generated and manual measurements and the effect of AI assistance on the consistency of measurements across users. Results: AI assistance reduced mean exam time by 2.23 minutes (SD 0.44 minutes) (95% CI: -3.10, -1.36; P<0.001); independent of participants age, experience, or the sequence of AI-assisted vs manual scans. AI assistance reduced mean distance traveled by the non-scanning hand by 49.2% (P<0.001). AI assistance also reduced overall control interactions by the non-scanning hand by 36%, touchscreen reaches by 41.5%, interactions with the control panel by 23.4%, and mouse movements and clicks by 54.2% and 61.1%, respectively (P<0.001 for all). During offline measurement, users accepted 94.3% of AI-generated measures without modification. AI assistance reduced inter-user measurement variability by 74%. Conclusions: AI assistance significantly reduced exam time and improved ergonomics compared with manual scanning and supported more standardized measurements across users. These findings support the integration of AI-assisted tools into imaging workflows to enhance workflow efficiency, ergonomics, and diagnostic consistency.

after.title: Preprint: The EEG-Respiratory Gap: a deep learning biomarker associated with long-term mortality in obstructive sleep apnea
after.authors: Lee, H. K.; Park, K.; Choi, Y. R.; Lee, D.-e.; Kim, H.-S.; Shin, H.-W.
after.abstract: The apnea-hypopnea index (AHI) summarizes respiratory events by frequency, but was not designed to reflect how strongly an individual's brain responds to them. We developed a deep-learning model that estimates AHI from a single EEG channel (AHIbrain), developed using 22,044 polysomnography recordings and validated in an internal test set (r=0.88) and three external test sets (r=0.50-0.62). From AHIbrain, we derived two complementary metrics that characterize the EEG-Respiratory Gap: {Delta}AHIbrain, reflecting whether a patient's AHIbrain is higher or lower than expected for their measured AHI, and AHIbrain,event-free, estimated from epochs without scored respiratory events. Both were associated with sleep macro-, micro-, and epoch-level EEG features, suggesting that this discrepancy is not solely attributable to model error. Among participants free of cardiovascular disease, both metrics were associated with all-cause and non-CVD mortality after adjustment for AHI and clinical risk factors. After accounting for the same covariates, AHIbrain,event-free was also associated with CVD mortality in the highest-versus-lowest quartile comparison. These findings support the EEG-Respiratory Gap as an interpretable EEG-derived measure associated with prognostic information beyond AHI.

after.title: Preprint: LLM-generated patient-friendly discharge letters for newly diagnosed rheumatic and musculoskeletal diseases: a prospective feasibility study
